st.t: Citation errors: Genuine authorities can still mislead
st.an: The source accepts that legal AI can be useful only with human verification and materially develops the cluster’s proposition through a preregistered evaluation showing that retrieval reduces but does not eliminate errors. qs: LexisNexis claims that its AI tool provides “linked hallucination-free legal citations” (LexisNexis, 2023), but, as we demonstrate below, this claim can only be true in the most narrow sense of “hallucination,” in that their tool does indeed link to real legal documents.9 If those linked sources are irrelevant, or even contradict the AI tool’s claims, the tool has, in our sense, engaged in a hallucination.
Users of these tools must continue to verify that key propositions are accurately supported by citations.

kp.k: Legal research tools reduce but do not eliminate hallucinations
kp.d: The authors' empirical evaluation finds substantial hallucinations in all three proprietary legal research tools, despite vendor claims that retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) avoids or eliminates them. Figure 4 reports hallucination rates of 17% for Lexis+ AI, 33% for Westlaw AI-Assisted Research, 17% for Ask Practical Law AI, and 43% for closed-book GPT-4. These are findings for the tested 2024 products and benchmark, not estimates for every legal AI system or subsequent version.
qs: Commercially-available RAG-based legal research tools still hallucinate.
Over 1 in 6 of our queries caused Lexis+ AI and Ask Practical Law AI to respond with misleading or false information.
And Westlaw hallucinated substantially more—one-third of its responses contained a hallucination.

kp.k: Responsiveness materially changes comparisons of tool reliability
kp.d: Figure 4 reports accurate/incomplete/hallucinated responses respectively as 65%/18%/17% for Lexis+ AI, 42%/25%/33% for Westlaw, 20%/63%/17% for Ask Practical Law AI, and 49%/8%/43% for GPT-4. Nearby prose retains slightly different figures, while a validation footnote explicitly explains Practical Law's accuracy revision from 19% to 20%. The authors attribute Practical Law's low responsiveness to its narrower collection of attorney-authored practical guidance rather than comprehensive primary authorities. They find Lexis+ AI's hallucination rate significantly lower than the other legal tools even conditional on responding.
qs: Responsiveness differs dramatically across systems.
The low responsiveness of Ask Practical Law AI can be can be explained by its more limited universe of documents.
Westlaw AI-AR and Ask Practical Law AI respond to fewer queries than GPT-4, but the responses that they do produce are not significantly more trustworthy.

kp.k: Preregistered testing evaluates open-ended research and legal authority
kp.d: The study uses 202 queries: 80 general legal research, 70 jurisdiction- or time-specific, 22 false-premise, and 30 factual-recall questions. Twenty Rule QA questions came verbatim from LegalBench and twenty from BARBRI; the remaining 162 were handwritten or adapted. Registration occurred March 22, 2024; Lexis+ AI, Practical Law AI, and GPT-4 were tested March 22–April 22, and Westlaw May 23–27. GPT-4 used gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09 without external retrieval. Expert manual scoring included independent checking of 48 stratified responses, yielding Cohen's kappa 0.77 and 85.4% agreement. Although the supplied heading identifies a 2025 journal article, the reproduced manuscript describes itself as a June 3, 2024 updated preprint.
qs: We design a diverse set of legal queries to probe different aspects of a legal RAG system’s performance.
Queries on Westlaw’s AI-AR system were run between May 23–27, 2024.
A fourth labeler then labeled a random sample of 48 responses, stratified by model and task type.

kp.k: Real citations do not guarantee legally supported answers
kp.d: The authors distinguish correctness from groundedness: an answer can state a true proposition while falsely claiming that a cited source supports it. Their operational definition counts incorrect or misgrounded answers as hallucinations; correct but uncited answers and refusals are incomplete, while accurate answers must be both correct and grounded. Groundedness requires legally relevant authority, not merely fidelity to retrieved text. This broader research definition differs from vendor language focused narrowly on whether linked documents exist.
qs: A response is considered hallucinated if it is either incorrect or misgrounded.
In other words, if a model makes a false statement or falsely asserts that a source supports a statement, that constitutes a hallucination.
We code correct but ungrounded responses as incomplete because, unlike a misgrounded response, an ungrounded response does not actually make any false assertions.

kp.k: Legal interpretation creates failures beyond document retrieval
kp.d: Observed errors include reversing case holdings, confusing litigants' arguments with judicial decisions, misreading appellate hierarchy, treating overruled law as current, and fabricating legal provisions. The authors identify naive retrieval, inapplicable authority, reasoning errors, and sycophancy as overlapping contributing categories. Among hallucinated answers, Table 6 attributes reasoning errors to 28% for Lexis, 61% for Westlaw, and 49% for Practical Law. These causal classifications are provisional because proprietary architectures and the exact text passed to models are not observable. Suggested Westlaw citation suppression for overruled cases is explicitly a hypothesis, not an established system mechanism.
qs: Systems do not seem capable of consistently making out the holding of a case.
Systems can fail to distinguish between arguments made by litigants and statements by the court.
Because these are closed systems, we are not able to clearly identify a single point of failure for each hallucination.

kp.k: Human verification can erode promised research efficiency
kp.d: The authors argue that detecting subtle errors requires reading cited sources, assessing authority, and checking propositions rather than merely confirming citation existence. Westlaw's non-refusal answers averaged 350 words (SD 120), compared with Lexis+ AI's 219 (SD 114) and Practical Law's 175 (SD 67), creating more opportunities for response-level errors and more verification work. They connect this burden to competence and supervision under state-adopted versions of ABA Model Rules 1.1 and 5.3. The study does not quantify net productivity gains or losses.
qs: Checking for these kinds of hallucinations requires users to click through to cited references, read and understand the relevant sources, assess their authority, and compare them to the propositions the model seeks to support.
Lengthier answers also require substantially more time to check, verify, and validate, as every proposition and citation has to be independently evaluated.
Users of these tools must continue to verify that key propositions are accurately supported by citations.

kp.k: Benchmark results have substantial scope and temporal limitations
kp.d: The authors explicitly reject interpreting their challenging benchmark as an unbiased population-level hallucination estimate. Findings concern three proprietary research products at particular times, not Harvey, Vincent AI, CoCounsel memorandum drafting, contract review, or deposition summarization. They exclude conclusions about Lexis+ AI's subsequently released second generation. Other qualifications include the small sample, imperfect human agreement, evolving and potentially nondeterministic outputs, restricted interfaces, and possible test leakage. The authors also distinguish response accuracy from usefulness within a human research workflow.
qs: Our estimate of the hallucination rate is not meant to be an unbiased estimate of the (unknown) population-level rate of hallucinations in legal AI queries, but rather to assess whether hallucinations have in fact been solved by RAG, as claimed.
Second, our evaluation only captures a point in time.
Our results do not speak to the performance of this second generation product, if different.

kp.k: Opaque products impede professional oversight and equitable evaluation
kp.d: The authors recommend rigorous, transparent benchmarking and public evaluations, arguing that restricted access, limited technical documentation, and absent published performance results impede informed professional supervision. They report three initially denied requests for Westlaw access, subsequently granted after initial results were released. They cite Paul Weiss's unpublished internal Harvey evaluation as an example of well-resourced firms' ability to assess tools, and argue that unequal evaluation capacity qualifies claims about AI improving access to justice. This is a distributive argument, not a measured finding about unmet legal need.
qs: The most important implication of our results is the need for rigorous, transparent benchmarking and public evaluations of AI tools in law.
The company provided access after the initial release of our results.

If only well-heeled actors can even evaluate the risks of AI systems, claims of functionality (Raji et al., 2022) and that AI can improve access to justice may be quite overstated (Bommasani et al., 2022; Chien et al. 2024; Perlman, 2023; Tan et al., 2023).

kp.k: Vendor marketing and defective outputs may create legal exposure
kp.d: The authors warn that inconsistent or overstated hallucination-free claims may expose vendors to unfair-competition or misleading-advertising liability. They separately discuss emerging tort theories involving negligent release, vicarious liability, products liability, and defamation. These are potential legal implications and reported scholarly theories, not adjudicated liability findings against the tested vendors.
qs: First, companies must be careful not to overclaim or misrepresent the abilities of their AI products.

Without additional precision about the exact mistakes that their tools purportedly avoid, companies may find themselves exposed to civil liability for unfair competition or false, misleading, or unsubstantiated claims.
Second, legal AI providers must also be cautious about emerging theories of tort liability for AI-inflicted harms.

kp.k: Research augmentation remains promising despite unresolved reliability
kp.d: The authors do not conclude that legal AI lacks value. They identify semantic retrieval, reduced hallucination relative to GPT-4, and correction of faulty premises as promising capabilities. False-premise questions yielded the highest accuracy, and Lexis+ AI, Westlaw, and GPT-4 often corrected mistaken assumptions; Practical Law mostly refused such queries. Their recommended positioning is an initial research aid subject to human checking, rather than a final authoritative answer. Benefits relative to traditional research are presented as potential value rather than measured workflow outcomes.
qs: That said, even in their current form, these products can offer considerable value to legal researchers compared to traditional keyword search methods or general-purpose AI systems, particularly when used as the first step of legal research rather than the last word.
Semantic, meaning-based retrieval of legal documents may be of substantial value independent of how these systems then use those documents to generate statements about the law.
Ask Practical Law AI also seldom hallucinated in this category, but refused to answer at all in the overwhelming majority of queries.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Magesh and colleagues find that specialist legal research AI reduces, but does not eliminate, hallucinations; they argue that its value lies in supervised research assistance rather than authoritative answers.
pts.d: The authors report substantial differences among the tested products. Figure 4 reports hallucinated/accurate/incomplete responses of 17%/65%/18% for Lexis+ AI, 33%/42%/25% for Westlaw AI-Assisted Research, 17%/20%/63% for Ask Practical Law AI, and 43%/49%/8% for closed-book GPT-4. Nearby prose contains minor inconsistencies with these figures. Their definition of hallucination includes false statements and claims falsely attributed to cited sources, not merely nonexistent citations. They find errors involving holdings, distinctions between litigants and courts, and hierarchies of authority. They argue that subtle errors require extensive human verification, potentially undercutting promised efficiency gains, but do not measure net productivity. They nevertheless suggest that semantic retrieval and initial research guidance can provide considerable value. Further implications include difficulty fulfilling professional supervision duties when vendors withhold tool-specific evidence, potentially overstated access-to-justice benefits when evaluation resources are concentrated in wealthy firms, and possible advertising or tort liability for vendors. These last points are arguments and conditional legal-risk predictions, not measured market outcomes. Vendor promises of eliminating hallucinations are claims the authors challenge, not claims they endorse.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The central reliability findings rest on a preregistered, manually evaluated 202-query benchmark; broader professional, economic, and liability implications rely on interpretation, cited guidance, scholarship, and examples.
pts.d: The Stanford-led study tests three proprietary RAG-based legal research products against GPT-4 on 80 general research questions, 70 jurisdiction- or time-specific questions, 22 false-premise questions, and 30 factual-recall questions. The dataset includes 20 LegalBench Rule QA questions and 20 BARBRI questions verbatim, with the remaining 162 handwritten or adapted. Expert reviewers assessed correctness and support from applicable legal authority. A separate reviewer graded a stratified random sample of 48 responses, yielding Cohen's kappa of 0.77 and 85.4% agreement. Detailed examples document contradictory case summaries, inapplicable authorities, fabricated legal provisions, and failures to distinguish procedural actors. Proposed failure mechanisms are inferred from observable outputs and retrieved documents rather than established through access to internal systems. The verification-burden argument draws on these errors and response lengths, not a timed workflow experiment. Professional-duty implications cite Model Rules 1.1 and 5.3 and state bar guidance; liability predictions cite regulatory statements, scholarship, and the Canadian airline chatbot misrepresentation case rather than liability findings against the tested legal vendors. The distributive argument cites reporting about Paul Weiss's internal evaluation of Harvey, whose results were not public. Harvey itself was not tested in this study.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings describe specific products tested in spring 2024, not current or future product performance, and are not population-wide estimates of legal-AI error rates.
pts.d: Although the supplied document header identifies a 2025 journal publication, the reproduced manuscript identifies itself as a June 3, 2024 updated preprint. Preregistration occurred March 22, 2024. Lexis+ AI, Ask Practical Law AI, and GPT-4 queries were run March 22–April 22; Westlaw AI-Assisted Research was tested May 23–27. GPT-4 used gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09 without external retrieval. The authors expressly exclude the subsequently released second-generation Lexis+ AI from their conclusions. The deliberately challenging benchmark probes claims of hallucination elimination rather than estimating the unknown natural distribution of lawyers' queries. Rates are response-level: any false statement can make an answer incorrect, and a longer answer presents more opportunities for error. Correct but uncited responses and refusals are classified as incomplete, not hallucinated; partially correct responses without falsehoods are counted as correct. The comparison does not establish that every specialist tool's responsive answer is more trustworthy than GPT-4's, because refusal rates differ. Results do not extend to contract review, deposition summaries, open-ended memorandum drafting, or untested products. Future liability and access-to-justice implications have no quantified horizon and remain conditional; usefulness depends on the task and human interaction.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The authors identify consequences for practicing lawyers, research-tool vendors, firms with unequal evaluation resources, and lay users seeking legal help.
pts.d: Lawyers using these U.S.-focused research products gain potential research assistance but retain responsibility for checking propositions, citations, and governing authority. The authors connect this burden to competence and supervision under jurisdictionally adopted professional rules, rather than suggesting the ABA Model Rules automatically govern all lawyers. Clients are indirectly exposed when lawyers rely on inaccurate research, though client outcomes are not measured. LexisNexis and Thomson Reuters are treated as legal-technology vendors, not alternative legal service providers; they face pressure to substantiate marketing, permit meaningful evaluation, improve reliability, and consider potential liability. Well-resourced firms can undertake internal evaluations unavailable to less-resourced actors, potentially concentrating the ability to assess tools safely. Pro se litigants and lay parties may be especially vulnerable to tools accepting mistaken premises, although the study also finds that several tested systems often corrected false premises successfully. The authors therefore question unconditional access-to-justice promises, without concluding that AI cannot help address unmet civil legal need.
